summary: For ages 6-7, extend precision from words to symbols and units across three strands: (1) read '=' relationally as 'is the same as / both sides balance', not operationally as 'the answer comes next'; (2) always attach a unit to a measurement ('12 cm', not '12'); (3) use precise vocabulary for 3-D shapes (face, edge, vertex) and comparisons (greater than, less than). The equals-sign strand is the load-bearing one: Falkner, Levi & Carpenter documented that most primary children read '=' operationally, so a running chain like 7+5=12+3=15 looks correct to them. Confront this directly with true/false sentences, open number sentences, and a balance representation. A pan-balance interaction can make the meaning concrete, but a dialogue partner, a rotatable 3-D model, and screener items each serve distinct purposes and are preserved below.
misconceptions: Reads '=' operationally as 'the answer is / and then', writing running chains like 7+5=12+3=15 (Falkner/Levi/Carpenter)
Fills 8+4=□+5 with 12 (the total so far) or 17 (everything added), not 7
Omits units, giving '12' for a length that is 12 cm — treating the unit as optional (CCSS)
Describes 3-D shapes with 2-D or loose words — 'corner' for vertex, 'side' for face, or calls a cube a 'square'

activities.title: Weigh the sentence: does '=' balance?
steps: Take a friend's working, 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 = 15, and look only at the middle part: 7 + 5 = 12 + 3.

Using identical cubes (each cube weighs the same), place 7+5 cubes on the left pan and 12+3 cubes on the right pan of a pan balance and observe which way it tips (left holds 12 cubes, right holds 15, so the heavier right pan sinks and the lighter left pan rises — it does not balance).
Say aloud what '=' promises: both sides weigh the same.
Decide whether 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 is true or false, and explain using the balance.
Make both sides the same a different way, e.g. check that 3 + 5 = 6 + 2 (both are 8).
Complete an open sentence like 8 + 4 = □ + 5 by making the pans level, and say what number balances it (7).
activities.insight: The equals sign means the two sides are the same amount; it is not an arrow pointing to the next answer. A running chain like 7+5=12+3=15 misuses '='. A balance that tips or levels makes this relationship visible.

activities.title: '12 what?' — the unit is part of the answer
steps: Measure an object (e.g. a pencil) and give the measurement.
When you answer '12', state the unit: 12 what? Could it be 12 metres, 12 centimetres?
Compare 12 cm with 12 m aloud and say why the unit changes what the number means.
Write the measurement with its unit (e.g. '12 cm', '3 kg') and read it aloud.
activities.insight: A bare number does not say how much; the unit is part of the measurement answer and changes its meaning entirely (12 cm vs 12 m).

activities.title: Name and touch the parts of a 3-D shape
steps: Handle or rotate a 3-D solid (e.g. a cube-shaped block).
Point to and name each part: a face (a flat surface), an edge (where two faces meet), a vertex (a corner point).
Say which is which when asked to point to a face, an edge, and a vertex on the solid.
Use the precise words: say 'face' rather than 'side', learn 'vertex' as the mathematical name for a corner (corner is the everyday word), and do not call a cube a 'square'.
activities.insight: 3-D shapes have precise, named parts — face, edge, vertex — and a face is not the same as the 'side' of a flat shape; attaching the word to the felt feature is intended to help the vocabulary take hold.

activities.title: Convince the pedantic listener
steps: Talk with an in-role character (e.g. a robot or shopkeeper) who reads notation literally and only accepts true, fully specified statements.
When the character asks 'you said 12 — 12 what?', supply the unit.
When the character asks 'is 7 + 5 really the same as 12 + 3?', state whether it is true and why.
Repair any imprecise statement so the literal-minded listener accepts it.
activities.insight: Precise symbol and unit use is what makes a statement unambiguous to a listener; explaining and repairing out loud may deepen the child's reasoning behind '=' and units.

activities.title: True/false and unit-completion screener
steps: Sort number sentences as true or false, including items like 'is 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 true?'.
Complete 'add the unit' items where a bare number must be given its unit.
Flag any sentence that misuses '=' as a running total.
activities.insight: Quick true/false and unit items can reveal the operational-equals error and the missing-unit habit, signalling who needs the fuller balance and dialogue work.

checkQuestion: A child worked out 7 + 5 + 3 by writing: 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 = 15. Look just at the middle part, 7 + 5 = 12 + 3. Is that a true sentence? What does the '=' sign promise about the two sides?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that '=' means the two sides are the same, so 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 is NOT true (12 is not 15), even though the child was correctly doing the steps; the chain misuses '=' as 'and then'. Surfaced for discussion, not marked.
